frontmatter.title: Participant-Level Estimates of Structure Use, Strategies and Couplings

children.value: The structure-use models, the placement strategies after events and the mouse-tracking analyses describe effects at the level of the group. This chapter estimates the same effects within each participant: the structure-use models with by-participant random slopes for every within-participant term, the strategies as participant profiles with their reliability, the persistence of a strategy after it worked, and the couplings of cursor and gaze with the model uncertainty before the outcome as within-participant slopes. The dependence of a within-participant effect on the questionnaire scores is tested as a cross-level interaction in the mixed model where participants contribute few observations, and as a regression of the participant slopes on the score where they contribute many. The participant estimates are saved as features for later analyses.
) and STICSA trait, z-scored. Condition contrasts as in the other chapters (Full versus None and Partial, Partial versus None).
The models S1 to S5 of
Use of the Two-State and Temporal Structure

were refitted with by-participant random slopes for all within-participant terms, and S5 additionally with the continuous position in the session (trial, per 100 trials) instead of the session half (S5c). The random-effect structure was selected from the maximal one downward (Matuschek et al., 2017): structures that did not converge or were singular were skipped, and of two nested structures the larger one was kept if the likelihood-ratio test gave p < .20. All candidate fits are listed in

. The score dependence of each within-participant term was tested as a cross-level interaction (term × score), with the selected structure and with random intercepts only. Participant estimates are the fixed effect plus the conditional mode of the random slope; their reliability is var(conditional modes) / (var(conditional modes) + mean conditional variance).

Participants differ detectably in how often they place nets at alternative directions (direction, position in episode, session half) and in how much more they follow transitions than oddballs at t+1. They do not differ detectably in the dependence of following an oddball on its direction or on the time since the last transition, or in the dependence of following a transition on the length of the preceding episode: for these terms the variance of the participant slopes was estimated at or near zero, so individual estimates of temporal-structure use cannot be obtained from these binary event outcomes with about 16 oddballs and 8 transitions per participant.
Score terms with the selected structure (general factor, log-odds per SD):

With random intercepts only, nets at alternative directions decreased more steeply over the episode in higher scorers (general factor −0.24, SE = 0.056, p < .001; STICSA trait −0.26, p < .001). With the selected random slopes the estimate is smaller and its standard error twice as large (−0.18, SE = 0.102, p = .072; STICSA trait −0.18, p = .081): the participants’ own slopes of position vary, and the score association is not separable from that variation.
S5, event type × score at t+1.

The smaller difference between transitions and oddballs in higher scorers is of the same size with the random slope of the session half added (general factor −0.24, SE = 0.126, p = .055; STICSA trait −0.25, SE = 0.125, p = .043) as with random intercepts only (−0.23, p = .042; −0.24, p = .030). The same holds with the continuous trial (general factor −0.24, p = .059).

No random slope was supported, so both forms coincide: −0.27 (SE = 0.134, p = .042) for the general factor and −0.25 (p = .067) for STICSA trait, a smaller advantage of oddballs toward the other latent state in higher scorers.

The remaining cross-level terms (S2 direction, S3a, S3b, S4, S5 at t+2, and the change of following over the session or over trials) were all p ≥ .15. With BH correction over the 17 cross-level terms of the nine models (S1, S2, S3a, S3b, S4, S5 and S5c at t+1 and t+2), separately for each score and each random-effect form, no term is below q = .05 with the selected structure (smallest q = .31 for the general factor, .35 for STICSA trait).

The participant estimates are most reliable for the session-half and position terms of S2 (.66 and .62) and for the difference between transitions and oddballs in following at t+1 (.53 to .54), and less reliable for the difference at t+2 (.35 to .36), for direction in S2 (.31), for the change of commitment over the session (.30) and for the change of following over the session or the trials (.27 to .28). For each participant, the share of each placement class at t+1 (as in
Responses to Events and Placement Duration

) was computed separately after transitions (on average 8 per participant) and after oddballs (on average 16), together with the selectivity, the share of transitions followed minus the share of oddballs followed. The reliability of each share is the Spearman–Brown corrected correlation between the odd- and even-numbered events of the type. Score associations: share (z) ~ score (z) + condition, OLS with HC3, BH over the 13 measures per score.

Following and splitting after transitions and all classes after oddballs except diffuse placements are moderately stable properties of a participant (r_SB .53 to .66). Staying, partial and third-direction placements after transitions are not (r_SB .11 to .17); with about eight transitions per participant their shares are dominated by sampling noise. The selectivity has a reliability of .44 (mean .09, SD .23).

Higher scores went with a lower selectivity (general factor −0.19 SD per SD [−0.35, −0.02], p = .025, q = .16; STICSA trait −0.19 [−0.35, −0.04], p = .014, q = .18), the participant-level counterpart of the smaller difference between transitions and oddballs in following at t+1 in the trial-level model. A higher general factor also went with more placements at the third direction after transitions (0.21 [0.05, 0.36], p = .010, q = .13), a share with a reliability of .17. No association reached q < .05 (BH over the 13 measures, separately for each score).
Persistence of a strategy after it worked

children.label: Persistence of a strategy after it worked

children.value: For 2,165 pairs of consecutive events of 96 participants,

is whether the placement at t+1 of the next event has the same class as at the current event. Model: repeat ~ blocked_w + blocked_b + same event type + class + condition + (1 + blocked_w | participant), logistic, with blocked_w whether the attack on the t+1 trial was blocked, centred within the participant, and blocked_b the participant’s share of blocked t+1 attacks.

The class was repeated at 30 % of the next events (34 % after a blocked attack at t+1, 28 % after a bite). With the class and the event type in the model, a blocked attack did not make the repetition more likely within participants (0.11 log-odds, SE = 0.13, p = .40); repetitions were more frequent when the next event was of the same type (0.32, p = .003) and differed between the classes. The within-participant effect of a blocked attack did not depend on the scores (general factor × blocked_w 0.01, p = .91; STICSA trait 0.05, p = .70). The strategy chosen after an event thus does not follow a win-stay pattern across events.

Cursor and gaze against the model uncertainty

children.label: Cursor and gaze against the model uncertainty

children.value: The uncertainty before the outcome of a trial (predictive entropy and state uncertainty of Nexus, the uncertainty of the change-point observer and of the n-state model) was related to the cursor and gaze measures of the same trial: y ~ x_within + x_between + trial + condition + (1 + x_within | participant), linear mixed model (ML), with x_within the uncertainty centred within the participant and x_between the participant mean, both divided by the SD of the uncertainty across trials, and y z-scored. Where the model with the random slope did not converge, the random intercept model is reported (column

; 10 of 40 models). Participant slopes: OLS of y on x_within and trial per participant (at least 40 trials); slope (z) ~ score (z) + condition, OLS with HC3. BH over the 16 cursor models (4 measures × 4 uncertainty signals) and over the 24 gaze models (6 × 4); for the participant slopes, over the same 16 or 24 slopes separately for each score.

Within participants, higher uncertainty went with more curved first movements and more direction changes of the cursor (state uncertainty of Nexus 0.08 and 0.08 SD per SD, n-state model 0.07 and 0.08, all q < .001), a slightly earlier start of the movement (−0.03 to −0.04) and a cursor that covered more of the circle during the cue (state uncertainty 0.13, n-state 0.10). The predictive entropy of Nexus had the opposite sign for the cursor (curvature −0.11, direction changes −0.17, cursor entropy during the cue −0.40). For the gaze, higher uncertainty went with less fixation time at the current state during placement (Nexus entropy −0.17, state uncertainty −0.15, change-point −0.14) and more at the other state (0.29, 0.13, 0.11) and beyond the states (0.21, 0.13, 0.13), and with a higher gaze entropy during placement (state uncertainty 0.15, n-state 0.13). These couplings were present in most participants (for example, gaze at the other state with Nexus entropy positive in 82 %, gaze at the current state with state uncertainty negative in 92 %, gaze entropy during placement with state uncertainty positive in 95 %).

No participant slope was associated with a score at q < .05. The largest associations: participants with higher general-factor scores showed fewer additional cursor direction changes under higher state uncertainty (−0.30 [−0.51, −0.09], p = .006, q = .09; STICSA trait −0.24, p = .007, q = .11), and more additional fixations during the cue (0.24 [0.06, 0.41], p = .009, q = .19).
